story: Bahram Gur Slays a Dragon, a Shahnama page now at the Cleveland Museum of Art. It comes from the Great Mongol Shahnama, painted in Tabriz around 1330 to 1335. Bahram Gur, who reigned 420 to 438 CE, was a Sasanian ruler and great hunter. He took the name Gur, meaning onager, a wild ass, because it was his favourite game. He also slew dragons. The rocks, tree and dragon borrow from Chinese painting styles.

story: The text page of Bahram Gur Arrives at the House of a Merchant, from the same sheet as Bahram Gur Slays a Dragon. It comes from the Great Mongol Shahnama, painted in Tabriz around 1330 to 1335. Bahram Gur, who reigned 420 to 438 CE, was a Sasanian ruler and great hunter. He took the name Gur, meaning onager, a wild ass, because it was his favourite game. He also slew dragons.

story: This bottle looks medieval, but it was made in Europe around 1900. Its bold writing praises Muhammad ibn Qala'un, a Mamluk sultan of Egypt who died in 1341. In the late 1800s, Europeans became fascinated by Islamic art, and glassmakers revived the enamelling and gilding that made Mamluk glass famous. Some copies were honest tributes, others were sold as fakes. Either way, it shows how one era's art can be reborn centuries later, far from where it began, by people trying to understand how it was done.

story: This bottle was made in Iran more than a thousand years ago, and the pattern around its body and neck was carved straight into the glass. Its dark blue-green colour would have glowed when light passed through it. Cutting decoration into glass like this, as if it were hard stone, was a tradition the Islamic world took over from Sasanian Persia, and it was at its most popular between the 9th and 11th centuries.

locator: Commons search="caravanserai"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 4.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This huge courtyard in the desert was a safe stop for travellers for over a thousand years. Deir-e Gachin caravanserai sits in Kavir National Park, between Qom and Varamin, on the old road from Rey to Isfahan. It was first built in Sasanian times and repaired again and again under later dynasties; its current form is mostly Safavid. People call it the Mother of Iranian Caravanserais. In 2023 it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing with 53 other Persian caravanserais. Think of it as a medieval motorway service station, built to last.

title: Three treatises on astronomy by Karim Khan Kirmani (d. 1871), signed Muhammad Jawad bin Muhammad 'Ali al-Kirmani, Qajar Iran, dated January-February 1895
locator: Commons search="Islamic astronomy instrument"; LicenseShortName="Public domain"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This 1895 book is a do-it-yourself guide to the sky. It binds together three treatises by Karim Khan Kirmani, a 19th-century Iranian scholar who wrote on everything from medicine to optics and music. One explains the calendar in tables, one explains how to use and make an astrolabe, and one is a manual for a ring-shaped instrument. Even its painted lacquer cover shows an astrolabe quadrant. It came with two lacquered paper instruments, one probably the ring itself. Astronomy here is not just theory, it is something you hold in your hands.

story: Before clocks, how did a mosque know exactly when to pray? This book, by the astronomer Ibn al-Sufi who died in 1319, is a manual for timekeepers called muwaqqits. It shows how to tell the time and find the direction of Mecca from the sun's height, its angle and the length of shadows. The author says rulers and compasses alone are inaccurate, so he teaches the maths instead, using tables based on al-Farghani, a 9th-century astronomer. It is a reminder that daily prayer helped push science forward.

title: NGC3156 - Measure of a great galactic disc (potw2337a)
locator: Commons search="Islamic astronomy instrument"; LicenseShortName="CC BY 4.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This Hubble picture shows NGC 3156, a galaxy about 73 million light-years away. It is lenticular, which means lens-shaped, halfway between a round elliptical galaxy and a spiral. It sits in Sextans, a small constellation named after the sextant, a tool sailors and astronomers used to measure angles.

title: Southwestern Saudi Arabia at Night (9495028083)
locator: Commons search="Islamic astronomy instrument"; LicenseShortName="Public domain"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: Astronauts on the International Space Station took this night photo of the coast of southwestern Saudi Arabia in 2013. NASA says much of the country is dark at night because large areas of desert have few people. The south-west is different. Its milder climate supports several big cities, and their lights glow through patchy cloud near Abha and Khamis Mushait. A whole region's lifestyle, readable from orbit.

title: Smoke and sulfur dioxide plumes in Iraq (MODIS 2016-10-28)

scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: A NASA satellite photo of Iraq on 21 October 2016. Dark, oily smoke and sulfur dioxide pour from fires at the Qayyarah oil field, south of Mosul. ISIL had held the field since 2014. When Iraqi forces moved to retake it in June 2016, the wells were set on fire. War, visible from space.

title: Remains of an Arabic newspaper in Al Kharrara
locator: Commons search="Arabic newspaper"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 3.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: Somewhere in the desert of Al Kharrara in southern Qatar, Alex Sergeev found the remains of an Arabic newspaper and photographed them on 19 March 2013. Someone's news, left to the sand and the sun. The record gives no date for the paper itself, so we cannot tell which day's news it carried.

title: Arabic newspaper declare formation of the UAR, 1958
locator: Commons search="Arabic newspaper"; LicenseShortName="Public domain"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: In February 1958, Egypt and Syria joined to form one country, the United Arab Republic, and this Arabic newspaper announced it. Two countries became one state. The front page captures that moment before anyone knew how it would turn out. The photographer is unknown.

title: Sariaki Arabic script newspapers crop
locator: Commons search="Arabic newspaper"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 3.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: Saraiki newspapers printed in Arabic script, photographed by Ashashyou on 6 July 2013. The record says no more, so this one is light. There is nothing more in the record to go on.

title: Venus (newspaper)
locator: Commons search="Arabic newspaper"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 4.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This is the logo of Venus, a newspaper published in Nazareth from 1986 to 1988, so it lasted about three years. Irfan Shahid uploaded the image in 2015. The record says no more.

title: Text in Avar, arabic script, 1929
locator: Commons search="Arabic newspaper"; LicenseShortName="Public domain"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This newspaper text from 1929 is in the Avar language, written in Arabic script. Languages are not tied to one alphabet, and here Arabic letters are carrying a completely different language. The writer is anonymous.

title: Ibrahim al-Jaafari, Interview with Al Vefagh - 7 December 2017
locator: Commons search="Arabic newspaper"; LicenseShortName="CC BY 4.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This is Ibrahim al-Jaafari during an interview with the newspaper Al Vefagh on 7 December 2017. The record says no more about him or what he said, so this one is light.

title: Qazaq (kazakh) newspaper (1915)
locator: Commons search="Arabic newspaper"; LicenseShortName="Public domain"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This is the emblem of the newspaper 'Qazaq', Kazakh, from 8 January 1915. Esetok shared the image in 2013. The record says no more, so this one is light.

title: Astrolabe planisférique
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 3.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: A planispheric astrolabe, 10.2 cm across. It is in the Arab World Institute museum in Paris. Its main body and plate were made in Ottoman Turkey in 1098 AH, or 1686 to 1687, but its spider, the araignée, was added in the Maghreb around 1850. One brass tool, two places, over 160 years apart.

title: Islamic Astrolabe Doha
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 4.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: An Islamic astrolabe in the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha, Qatar, photographed by Ctac on 16 July 2018. The record names no maker or date for the instrument itself, so this one is light.

title: Islamic Astrolabe (28417763470)
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="CC0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This Islamic astrolabe is in the Gallery of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. Gary Todd photographed it on 1 August 2016. The record gives no maker or date for the astrolabe itself, so this one is light.

title: Spherical astrolabe islamic march 2024
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 4.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: Most astrolabes are flat discs. This one is a ball. It is a spherical Islamic astrolabe from about 1480, now in the Museum of the History of Science in Oxford, photographed by Geni in March 2024. The record gives no maker, but the shape alone makes it rare to see.

title: Astrolabe planisférique closeup800x600x300
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="CC BY-SA 3.0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: A close-up photo, from 2008, of a brass planispheric astrolabe. It is in the Arab World Institute museum in Paris. Its main body and plate were made in Ottoman Turkey in 1098 AH, or 1686 to 1687, but its spider, the araignée, was added in the Maghreb around 1850. One brass tool, two places, over 160 years apart.

title: Islamic Astrolabe (28084953514)
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="CC0"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: An Islamic astrolabe photographed by Gary Todd on 1 August 2016, in the same set as his photos from the Gallery of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.

title: Astrolabe Mortillaro
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="Public domain"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: In 1848, Vincenzo Mortillaro drew a 9th-century Abbasid astrolabe and printed it as a lithograph. So this is a 19th-century picture of a 1,000-year-old instrument: someone a thousand years later thought it worth copying exactly.

title: Britannica Astrolabe - Persian Astrolabe c.1712
locator: Commons search="Islamic astrolabe"; LicenseShortName="Public domain"
scope_basis: Commons file matched search; review needed
story: This drawing of a Persian astrolabe from about 1712 was published in 1911, in the Encyclopaedia Britannica according to the file's title. The artist is unknown. The record says no more.

title: Calligraphy Painting
summary: Non-illustrated single work; Opaque watercolor and ink on paste board
creator: Isma'il Jalayir
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1860"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This picture is writing and painting at once. Isma'il Jalayir made it in Iran around 1860, combining large flowing nasta'liq calligraphy with tiny scenes of court life and paradise-like gardens, all praising the ruler Nasir al-Din Shah. You have to look twice: first you read the words, then you notice the little worlds hidden in and around them. Here the art of the pen and the art of the brush share the same page.

title: Wall Painting
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="9th century"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A wall painting on plaster from Nishapur, Iran, in the 800s. Nishapur is now a city in northeast Iran. Painted walls this old rarely survive. This one came to the Met in 1940. The record says little more.

title: Botanical Painting: Geranium
summary: Illustrated single work; Opaque color on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1630"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This flower was painted so exactly that you could almost identify it in a garden. The Met's title is “Geranium”, and the page was made in India around 1630, in opaque colour on paper. At that time the Mughal emperor Jahangir, who died in 1627, had pushed his painters to record plants and animals with scientific care. Botanical studies like this sit between art and science, and they were admired and collected at court.

title: Botanical Painting: Dianthus
summary: Illustrated single work; Opaque color on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1630"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A dianthus flower, painted in India around 1630 as a botanical study, one flower given a whole page. It came from the collection of Howard Hodgkin, the British painter. The record says little more.

title: Botanical Painting: Composite Flower
summary: Illustrated single work; Opaque color on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1630"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A "composite flower", painted in India around 1630. Composite suggests the artist may have combined parts of several flowers into one. It came from the British painter Howard Hodgkin's collection of Indian art.

title: Painting of Alamgir Mosque
creator: Unknown
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="19th century"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A tiny painting of the Alamgir Mosque in Benares, now Varanasi, in ink on ivory. The mosque, also called Aurangzeb's Mosque, stands above the Panchaganga Ghat, whose broad steps go down to the Ganges. This 19th-century view was given to the Met in 2024.

title: Wall Painting with Female Figure
summary: Fragment of a wall painting; Stucco; painted
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="9th–10th century"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This fragment of a painted wall was found in a drain. It was dug up in the Sabz Pushan area of Nishapur and shows a female figure painted on plaster about 1,100 years ago. What scene she belonged to is now a mystery. Pieces like this are rare, because painted walls fall down, crumble or get painted over. Nishapur was wrecked by earthquakes and invasions that peaked in the 1200s, and the old city lay buried until the Met's team excavated there between 1935 and 1948.

title: Fragment of a Wall Painting
summary: Fragment of a wall painting; Stucco; painted
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 8th–early 9th century"; matched search q="painting"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A piece of painted wall plaster from Nishapur in Iran, from the late 700s or early 800s. It came to the museum in 1938. Painted walls rarely survive, so even a fragment is a glimpse of a lost room.

title: Page of Calligraphy
summary: Non-illustrated single work; Ink on dyed paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="dated 1075 AH/1664–65 CE"; matched search q="calligraphy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: Calligraphy from Turkey, dated 1664 to 1665, written in ink on dyed paper. The coloured paper is part of the design. The record says little more.

title: Page of Calligraphy
summary: Non-illustrated single work; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
creator: Muhammad Husain Kashmiri
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="early 17th century"; matched search q="calligraphy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A page of calligraphy written in India in the early 1600s by Muhammad Husain Kashmiri, with colour and gold. His name means he was from Kashmir. The museum record gives few other details.

title: Page of Calligraphy
summary: Folio from a non-illustrated manuscript; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="probably 15th century"; matched search q="calligraphy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A single page of calligraphy, probably from the 1400s, from Egypt or Iran. Even the museum is not sure which country. It is written in ink with colour and gold. Pages like this were often kept for the beauty of the hand alone. The record gives little more.

title: Page of Calligraphy
summary: Non-illustrated album leaf or single work; Ink on parchment
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="probably 16th–17th century"; matched search q="calligraphy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A page of calligraphy from Turkey, probably 1500s or 1600s, in ink on parchment. Just ink, no gold or colour: the writing has to do all the work. The record says little more.

title: Page of Calligraphy
summary: Non-illustrated album leaf; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
creator: Muhammad Shafi‘ known as Vesal-i Shirazi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="early–mid-19th century"; matched search q="calligraphy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A page of calligraphy from early 1800s Iran by Muhammad Shafi', known as Vesal-i Shirazi. His nickname links him to Shiraz. The page is decorated with colour and gold. The record gives few other details.

title: Page of Calligraphy
summary: Non-illustrated single work; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="17th century"; matched search q="calligraphy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A page of calligraphy from 17th-century India, with colour and gold around the writing. Pages like this were made to be looked at as art, not only read. The record does not name the writer.

title: Page of Calligraphy
summary: Non-illustrated album leaf; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
creator: Muhammad Husayn al-Katib
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 16th century"; matched search q="calligraphy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A page of calligraphy from late 1500s India by Muhammad Husayn al-Katib. "Al-Katib" simply means "the scribe". It is decorated with colour and gold. The record gives few other details.

title: Music Party on a Riverside Terrace
summary: Illustrated single work; Opaque color and gold on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1670"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A music party on a riverside terrace, painted in India around 1670 in colour and gold. It belonged to Howard Hodgkin, a British painter known for abstract art, who collected Indian paintings. His collection came to the Met, so a modern painter's eye picked this one.

title: "Night Scene: Group Listening to Music", Folio from the Davis Album
summary: Illustrated  album leaf; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 17th century"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A night scene from late 1600s India: a group of men listening to music. It is a page from the Davis Album, a collection left to the Met in 1915 by Theodore M. Davis. The artist had to show darkness and still let us see.

title: "A Scene of Dancing and Music", Folio from a Kulliyat (Complete Works) of Sa'di
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="19th century"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: Dancers and musicians fill this 19th-century Indian page from the complete works of Sa'di. Sa'di was a Persian Sufi poet of the 1200s, known for the depth of his thinking about society and morals. Six hundred years later, people in India were still painting his book.

title: "Bahram Gur Sees a Herd of Deer Mesmerized by Dilaram' s Music", Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
summary:
Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Main support: ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
Margins: gold on dyed paper
creator: Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="1597–98"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This painting is from a 1597–98 Indian copy of the Khamsa, or "Quintet", by the poet Amir Khusrau Dihlavi. It shows the king Bahram Gur watching a herd of deer stand still, spellbound by the music of Dilaram. It is ink, watercolour and gold on paper, with gold in the margins. A love story where music is strong enough to stop wild animals.

title: "Prince With his Courtiers and Musicians", Folio from the Davis Album
summary: Illustrated  album leaf; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="early 18th century"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A prince with his courtiers and musicians, painted in India in the early 1700s with colour and gold. It is a page from the Davis Album, left to the Met by Theodore M. Davis in 1915.

title: Kalamkari Rumal
summary: Cover; Cotton; plain weave, mordant painted and dyed, resist dyed
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1640–50"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This cloth was drawn and dyed by hand. It is a kalamkari rumal, a cotton cover made in Golconda in the Deccan around 1640–50. “Kalamkari” means pen-work: artists drew with a pen, used mordants so dyes would fix to the cotton, and resisted areas to keep them pale. The method uses only natural dyes and can take many steps. The Met lists birds, men, women and musicians on it. Golconda was a rich trading city, famous for diamonds as well as cloth.

title: Pair of Jeweled Anklets (Paijeb)
summary: Pair of  Anklets; Gold with inset jewels
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1850–1900"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: These gold anklets, set with jewels, were made in India between about 1850 and 1900. The Met calls them paijeb. Anklets are worn low, so they move with every step and catch the light as the wearer walks. Making a matching pair by hand means repeating every setting twice. This pair came to the Met as a gift from Princess Shamina Talyarkhan in 2024, so the museum's record of them is very new. The source gives little beyond this, so look closely at the settings yourself.

title: Two Folios from a Kitab-i Nauras (book of Nine Rasas) of Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II
summary: Folios from an illustrated manuscript; Black calligraphic ink, opaque watercolor, and gold paint on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1600"; matched search q="music"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: Here are two pages from a book by a sultan. Ibrahim Adil Shah II ruled Bijapur in southern India from 1580 to 1627. He was a poet and artist himself, and a generous patron of the arts. Under him the sultanate had its greatest period. These folios, from around 1600, come from his Kitab-i Nauras, the Book of Nine Rasas, written in black calligraphy with colour and gold. The Met bought them in 2025, so they are one of its newest arrivals.

title: Bottle in the Form of a Lute Player
summary: Figural vessel; Stonepaste; molded, turquoise-glazed, partially gilded
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="early 20th century"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This is a bottle shaped like a person playing a lute, moulded and glazed turquoise with touches of gold. Surprise: it is not ancient. The museum dates it to the early 1900s. The record does not say where it was made.

title: Turquoise Bowl with Lute Player and Audience
summary: Bowl; Stonepaste; glazed (opaque monochrome), in-glaze- and overglaze-painted, gilded
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 12th–early 13th century"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A musician plays the lute to a listening audience on a turquoise bowl made in Iran around 1200. The colour went on in two stages: some in the glaze, some over it, with gilding as well. Overglaze painting fired a second time was the new trick of mina'i ware, the first pottery to use overglaze enamels, made in Kashan until the Mongol invasion of 1219. The Met notes Arabic writing on the bowl too. Look for the listeners.

title: Bowl With Musicians in a Garden
summary: Bowl; Stonepaste; glazed in opaque white, luster-painted
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 12th–early 13th century"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: Women with lutes play music in a garden on this lustre bowl from Iran, made around 1200. The shine comes from a second firing of metallic paint with the oxygen cut off. So you would see a concert flicker as you turned the bowl in the light.

title: Mold Fragment with Musicians
summary: Mold fragment and modern cast; Earthenware; carved
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 11th–early 12th century"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This is a mould, a tool for making copies. Carved into the clay are musicians, and the potter would press soft clay into it to make raised pictures on pots, again and again. The Met has made a modern cast from it, so we can see the musicians the way they would have looked on a finished pot. It comes from Nishapur in Iran, around 900 years ago. It is a medieval printing press for pictures: one skilled carving, and then the same band of musicians could play on hundreds of pots.

title: "Isfandiyar's Fourth Course: He Slays a Sorceress", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Ink, opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on paper
creator: Abu'l Qasim Firdausi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1330–40"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: In the Shahnama, Iran's great epic, the hero Isfandiyar must pass seven trials. In the fourth, he kills a sorceress. This page, painted in Iran around 1330 to 1340 in ink, colour, gold and silver, shows that moment. Isfandiyar was a crown prince in the story, son of King Goshtasp.

title: Prince in a Garden Courtyard
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Opaque watercolor, ink, gold, and silver on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="1525–30"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This painting is a party frozen in time. Made in Tabriz in Iran around 1525 to 1530, it shows a prince seated under a canopy, holding a cup and a royal handkerchief, while attendants bring drinks and fruit and musicians play a lute called a barbat and a frame drum. Scenes like this, called bazm, showed the good life of the court: music, poetry and gardens. The artist used gold and silver on the page, so the scene would catch the light.

title: "Entertainment in a Garden", Folio from a Khamsa of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi, Matla' al-Anvar
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Opaque watercolor and gold on paper
creator: Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="second half 16th century"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A garden party painted in Iran in the late 1500s for the Matla' al-Anvar, the Rising of Lights, part of Amir Khusrau's Khamsa. Khusrau was a Sufi poet, singer and court musician in the Delhi Sultanate. His poems were copied and painted in Iran centuries later.

title: Shoulder of a Figure with Blue Drapery
summary: Fragment of a wall painting; Stucco; painted
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="9th–10th century"; matched search q="lute"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: The shoulder of a figure in blue clothes, painted on plaster in Nishapur, Iran, in the 800s or 900s. Only this piece is left of whoever it was. It came to the Met in 1938.

title: "Siyavush Plays Polo before Afrasiyab", Folio 180v from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Opaque watercolor, ink, silver, and gold on paper
creator: Abu'l Qasim Firdausi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1525–30"; matched search q="polo"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: Prince Siyavush plays polo in front of Afrasiyab, king of Turan and the main villain of the Shahnama. This page comes from the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, maybe the most fully illustrated copy ever made: 759 pages with 258 paintings by the royal workshop in Tabriz. It was given to the Ottoman Sultan Selim II in 1568, then broken up in the 1970s, so its pages are now scattered around the world.

title: "Siyavush Displays his Skill at Polo before Afrasiyab," Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings)
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
creator: Abu'l Qasim Firdausi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="dated 741 AH/1341 CE"; matched search q="polo"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This page shows a prince showing off at polo, painted in Shiraz in 1341. The story comes from the Shahnama, the Book of Kings, an epic poem by Ferdowsi of some 50,000 couplets, one of the longest poems ever written by one person. Ferdowsi spent about 33 years on it and finished in 1010. Here the hero Siyavush plays in front of Afrasiyab, king of Iran's great rival land. The book this page came from was later taken apart, and its pages are now spread among many museums.

story: Goats and horses run around this candlestick, picked out in silver against dark brass. It was made in Iran or Iraq in the first half of the 1300s. The craftsman cast the brass, engraved the design, and then hammered silver and a black compound into the cut lines. The result is a light-and-dark picture that changes as the candle flame moves. Candles were precious, and a stand this fine turned lighting a room into a small show.

story: This embroidered cloth from Gujarat in India could cover a bed or hang on a wall. Made in the 1600s from cotton stitched with silk, and once quilted, it is full of flowers. This piece once belonged to Ashburnham House in Sussex, England, and came to the Met from the Victoria and Albert Museum in 1954. Its journey from an Indian workshop to an English country house, then to New York, shows how far a beautiful cloth can travel.

title: Bustan (Orchard) of Sa'di

story: This book is a 500-year-old copy of a 770-year-old best seller. The Bustan, or Orchard, by the Persian poet Saadi was finished in 1257. It is a book of short stories and advice about justice, kindness, love and humility, a bit like Aesop's fables. This copy was written out in Bukhara in 1522 to 1523 by the calligrapher Mir 'Ali al-Husaini, in the flowing nasta'liq script, with coloured panels and five paintings. People kept copying Saadi for centuries because what he said about being a good person never went out of date.

story: This hunting horn is carved ivory, fitted with gilded silver mounts, and was made in India in the 1700s. Horns like this, called oliphants, were blown to send signals across open country during a hunt. It was also a showpiece: the carving and silver show that its owner wanted it to look as impressive as it sounded. Today elephants are protected and the ivory trade is tightly limited, so objects like this are history, not something to copy. The Met received it from J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917.

story: This velvet was made for a tent. It was woven around 1540, probably in Tabriz, from silk with flat metal thread. Velvet has a soft pile made from extra threads that are cut. Here some areas are left uncut or bare, so the hunters, horses and lions stand out against the background. It comes from the Safavid period, a high point of Persian art. Imagine a tent wall like this catching the light from lamps at night.

story: This silk is about 1,400 years old. It was woven in Syria in the early 600s, around the time Islam began. The Met tags it with horses, lions, and a bow and arrow: a hunt. Hunting scenes on silk and silver were a favourite of the Sasanian empire of Iran, whose art mixed old Persian ideas with influences from as far as China and the Mediterranean. A fragment this old is rare, and it shows how designs crossed borders long before the internet.

title: Ewer with Inscriptions and Hunting Scenes

story: This bronze jug is a hunting story you could pour from. Around its body a man and his saluki dog chase a hare, and another man fights a lion, all set among curling vines. Arabic writing wishes blessings and good fortune on its owner. It was made around the 11th century and dug up in Nishapur, then one of the great cities of Iran, rivalling Baghdad and Cairo for a time. Everyday things like this let us see what people there enjoyed, feared and hoped for, written and drawn in metal.

title: Planispheric Astrolabe

story: This astrolabe is the whole visible sky folded into a brass disc you can hold in one hand. Its maker's name, Muhammad Zaman al-Munajjim al-Asturlabi, ends in two job titles: astronomer and astrolabe-maker. He made it in Mashhad, Iran, in 1654–55, from pierced and engraved brass and steel. Sight a star, turn the plates, and it gives you the time or your latitude, or tells you which star you are looking at. Astrolabes were used from ancient Greece through the Islamic world to medieval Europe, and they led on to the sextant.

title: Astrolabe of ‘Umar ibn Yusuf ibn ‘Umar ibn ‘Ali ibn Rasul al-Muzaffari

story: This brass star-reader carries the name of a king. ʿUmar ibn Yusuf, the third sultan of the Rasulid dynasty in Yemen, was also a mathematician, astronomer and physician, and the Met names him as its maker. It is dated 690 AH, or 1291 CE. An astrolabe is a model of the sky you can hold. Sight the sun or a star through it, turn its plates, and it will tell you the time or your latitude, or name a star. It is brass, inlaid with silver. Picture a ruler who ran a country by day and studied the sky at night.

story: This brass tray was made in Cairo for a sultan who ruled Yemen, so it links two courts across the Red Sea. It is inlaid with silver and signed by Ahmad ibn Husayn al-Mawsili, a name meaning “from Mosul”, a city in northern Iraq. The Met dates it to about 1296–1321, during the reign of the Rasulid sultan al-Mu'ayyad. The Rasulids ruled Yemen for more than two centuries. One tray connects a craftsman from Iraq, a workshop in Egypt and a king in Yemen.

title: Inkwell with Zodiac Signs

story: Writers once kept their ink in brass pots decorated with the signs of the zodiac. This inkwell, probably made in Iran in the early 1200s, is cast in brass and inlaid with silver, copper and a black filling, so pale metal pictures stand out against the darker brass. The Met tags its decoration as zodiac. Every time a scribe dipped a pen, the twelve signs of the sky's yearly circle sat around the ink. It shows how a writing tool and a picture of the cosmos were combined in one object.

story: Before digital scales, markets ran on lumps of metal that everyone agreed to trust. This lead weight comes from Nishapur in northeast Iran and dates to the 800s or 900s. At the time Nishapur was one of the four great cities of Khorasan and a stop on trade routes from Central Asia, China, Iraq and Egypt. A weight like this let a buyer and a seller agree how much was on the scale. It is small and plain, yet that great city's trade relied on things like it.

story: This small glass disc was an anti-cheating device. It is a coin weight from Egypt, dated 808–810. It's easy to shave a little metal off the edge of a gold or silver coin, so traders checked coins against a trusted weight like this one. If a coin was lighter than the weight, someone had been trimming it. The Met's record tags the weight with Arabic, the language stamped on it. Fair weights meant fair trade, and markets depended on people trusting them.

story: This silver coin is a tiny newspaper from 983. Its writing says it was struck in Bukhara, names the Samanid ruler Nuh ibn Mansur and the Abbasid caliph al-Tali' lillah, and circles them with verses from the Qur'an. No pictures, just words, because on coins like this the writing was the decoration. It was found in Nishapur in Iran, far from where it was struck. Samanid coins travelled much further than that: thousands of them have turned up in the Baltic and Scandinavia, carried along the trade routes that linked Central Asia with northern Europe.

story: This gold coin carries a sign of the zodiac instead of a month. The Mughal emperor Jahangir believed in astrology. He issued a series of gold and silver coins showing zodiac signs against a radiating sun, with the sign standing in for the month the coin was minted. This one was struck in Agra in 1619, and the Met tags it with a bull, the sign of Taurus. A ruler's beliefs ended up in people's pockets.

title: Garden Carpet

story: This carpet is a garden you can walk on. It was woven around 1800 in northwestern Iran or Kurdistan, with wool pile on a cotton base. Garden carpets draw on the Persian charbagh, a garden split into four parts that was meant to picture an earthly utopia where people live in harmony with nature. In Iranian culture carpets were woven everywhere, by nomads, in villages and in royal workshops, for homes and for sale. On a carpet like this, the garden could come indoors and never fade.

story: This carpet is a garden you can walk on. Woven in Kurdistan in Iran in the second half of the 1700s, it lays out a formal garden as seen from above, with plants divided by channels of water. Gardens mattered deeply in Iran. The old Persian word for an enclosed garden, pairi-daeza, travelled through Greek and Latin into English as the word paradise. So a garden carpet brings a small paradise indoors, green and blooming, even in the middle of winter or a dry summer.

The gardens of the region were influenced by the Persian charbagh, a four-part garden meant to picture an earthly utopia where people live in harmony with nature. Water was what brought such a garden to life, and a fountain like this would have given it sound and movement. Imagine it running on a hot afternoon.

story: This is a carpet with a name that makes you look twice: the “Bird” carpet. It was knotted in wool, probably in western Turkey in the 1600s, with symmetrical knots tied one by one around the warp threads. Each knot is a single dot of colour, so the pattern was built up row by row like pixels on a screen. The weaver had to hold the whole design in mind while working on one small line at a time. Look closely and see where the “birds” might be.

story: These little bronze birds were made to sit on top of things, perhaps lids or containers, in Nishapur about a thousand years ago. The Met's team dug them up there between 1935 and 1940. Nishapur was a busy city on the road linking Iran with Central Asia and China, and its excavations turned up the details of daily life: lamps, inkwells, toys, jewellery and decorations like these. Somebody chose birds to perch on their everyday things, which tells you they wanted ordinary objects to be a little bit delightful.

story: This bird is woven, not painted. It sits in a circle of wool and linen about the size of your palm, made in Egypt around the 9th century using tapestry weaving, where coloured threads build the picture as the cloth grows. Egypt's Christian Coptic weavers were already famous for tapestry textiles before Islam, and the skill carried on afterwards. That a palm-sized patch of cloth has survived more than a thousand years is remarkable.

story: This bird is an incense burner. Smoke curled out through the holes cut into its body. It was cast in bronze, pierced and engraved in Central Asia or eastern Iran in the 1100s or 1200s. Incense filled rooms with scent, and a burner like this let the smoke escape in a pattern while the bird kept its shape. Khurasan, the wider region, was home to many of the great cities of the time. Imagine it sitting in a room and breathing out sweet smoke.

story: A single bird, studied so closely you can almost feel its feathers. Riza-yi ʿAbbasi painted it in Isfahan in 1634, about a year before he died, using ink, watercolour, gold and silver. Riza was the leading painter of Shah ʿAbbas I's court and is called the last great master of the Persian miniature. He helped change painting from crowded book scenes to single figures made for albums. People collected these pages, much as some people collect prints today.

story: This oil lamp is shaped like a bird. It was cast in bronze in Khurasan, in eastern Iran, around 1200, then engraved and inlaid with silver and copper. Oil went inside, a wick burned at the spout, and the bird glowed. Khurasan was a large historical region that is now split between Iran, Afghanistan and Central Asia. Its metalworkers turned a simple everyday thing into a small sculpture you could sit on a shelf.

story: This is a bath scraper, a medieval version of a scrubbing mitt. It was moulded from unglazed clay in Iran in the 1100s or 1200s. The rough clay was meant for the bathhouse. The hammam, a steam bath carried on from Roman baths, was central to life across the Islamic world. People used it to wash before prayer and to keep clean in an age before home plumbing, and it was also a place to meet friends. A small clay tool like this was part of a weekly routine for many people.

title: "Preparing Medicine from Honey", from a Dispersed Manuscript of an Arabic Translation of De Materia Medica of Dioscorides
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper

source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This page is from a medicine book that was already more than a thousand years old when it was painted. The Greek doctor Dioscorides wrote De materia medica between 50 and 70 CE. It covers about 600 plants and around 1,000 medicines. This Arabic copy was made in 1224, probably in Baghdad, and the painter ʿAbdullah ibn al-Fadl shows medicine being made from honey. Copies like this carried Greek knowledge through the Arabic-speaking world. From the 1500s the book also became the base for European herbals.

story: Before glass mirrors existed, people looked into polished metal. This cast bronze mirror comes from northwestern Iran or Turkey, from the 1100s or 1200s. One side was polished bright to reflect a face. The other side was decorated, and the Met tags the decoration with demons. The decorated back was what people saw when the mirror wasn't in use, so it had to be worth looking at too. Checking your reflection is a very old habit, and this is one of the tools people used.

story: The word “alembic” is Arabic, al-inbiq, and it came from an older Greek word for a cup. An alembic is a still: you heat a liquid, the vapour rises into a head like this one, cools, and runs out of the spout as a purer liquid. This one is green glass, blown by hand in Nishapur, Iran, between the 800s and 1000s. Glass-makers in the Islamic world built on Egyptian, Persian and Roman skills, and tools like this sat on the benches of early chemists. Today labs separate liquids the same way.

story: This stone mortar has a bowl at both ends, so it can do two jobs. It was made in 17th-century India. Before machines, mortars and pestles were how kitchens and healers ground spices, herbs and medicines. With two sides you could keep two powders apart, so one flavour or remedy didn't get into the next. Your kitchen may still have a smaller cousin of this tool. The source gives little more, so look closely at how the two bowls are shaped.

story: Men tread grapes, their feet doing the work a press does today. This page comes from a 1224 Arabic copy of Dioscorides' De materia medica, painted by ʿAbdullah ibn al-Fadl, possibly in Baghdad. Dioscorides, a Greek doctor in the Roman army, wrote the book in the first century CE to explain which plants heal and how. Painters like this one turned instructions into scenes of everyday work. The book itself was read for more than 1,500 years, in Greek, Latin and Arabic.

story: This bowl comes from Raqqa in Syria, made between the late 1100s and the 1200s. It is lustreware: after the first firing, the potter painted on metallic compounds and fired it again with the oxygen shut out, which leaves a shimmering metal-like shine. Raqqa's lustre pottery was a mainstay of the town's economy. In the 20th century, digs at Raqqa linked surviving pieces to the town.

title: Luster Ware Fragment

story: This broken piece shows how a technique travelled from Iraq to Spain. It comes from Valencia in the 1400s. Lustre, a shining metallic finish, was invented by potters in 9th-century Iraq. Potters in Muslim Spain brought it to Europe, and potters kept making it after Christian rulers took over the region. Valencian lustreware, especially from Manises, became the most luxurious pottery made in Europe and was exported far and wide. Then Italian maiolica caught up.

story: The Met calls this bowl “imported”. It was made in Iraq in the 900s, and the title tells us it ended up somewhere else. It is lustreware, pottery with a thin metallic film fired onto the glaze so it shines like gold. Potters in Iraq invented the technique in the early 800s, and by the 900s they liked bold designs built around one or two large figures. The Met tags this one with a woman. Shining bowls like this were luxury goods that travelled with traders.

Lustre is made by painting metallic compounds onto a fired pot and firing it again with the oxygen shut out, which leaves a metal-like shimmer. Someone later gave it silver fittings, so it was treasured enough to be dressed up.

story: Light shines through this glass bowl from about a thousand years ago. It was probably made in Fatimid Egypt, and its decoration was stained onto the glass. Its panelled walls and stylised palm-tree shapes echo Fatimid lustre bowls, and a band of angular Arabic writing runs round the rim. Nobody has managed to read that writing yet. A glass bowl this delicate surviving ten centuries is a small miracle in itself.

title: "The Father's Advice Followed by a Son who Sets out to Join a Caravan with the Two Oxen", Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
summary: Folio from an illustrated manuscript; Ink and opaque watercolor on paper

story: A father gives his son advice, and the son sets off to join a caravan with two oxen. It is a scene from Kalila wa Dimna, a set of animal fables full of lessons about life and politics. The stories came from India's ancient Panchatantra and travelled across the Middle East. This page was painted in India in the second quarter of the 1500s, so the stories had come home.

story: This is the hero Isfandiyar killing Arjasp, painted around 1330 to 1340 for a copy of the Shahnama, the Persian Book of Kings. In the epic, Isfandiyar is a legendary crown prince of Iran. The page uses ink, colour, gold and silver. Painters were turning a 50,000-couplet poem into pictures one scene at a time.

title: Panel from a Tent Lining

story: Imagine an emperor's palace that could be packed up and carried. This cotton panel, made in Burhanpur in India in the 1600s, probably lined one of the tents of a Mughal imperial camp. Mughal rulers moved with temporary camps, and textiles like this turned canvas into rooms fit for a ruler. It is more than two metres tall, one of a series that would have stood side by side like painted walls. A city of cloth could go up in one place, then come down and be rebuilt somewhere else.

title: Luster Bowl with Four Camels

story: Four camels walk across this bowl, and in the light the paint shines like metal. That shine is lustre, a thin layer of metal compounds fired onto the glaze. Potters in Iraq invented it in the early 800s. By the 900s, when this bowl was made, Iraqi lustre often showed one or two big figures, as here. The trick spread to Egypt, Syria, Iran and Spain, partly because pottery that looks like gold or silver was a respectable stand-in for real metal tableware.

story: A copper ewer from Turkey, dated 1707. A dated piece is useful: it pins down when its style was in use. The record says little more.

title: Portrait of a Dervish
summary:
Illustrated  album leaf; Main support: ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
Margins: gold on dyed paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="16th century"; matched search q="portrait"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This small painting shows a dervish, a Sufi who chose a simple life to come closer to God. It was painted in Bukhara in the 1500s and mounted as an album page, with gold-flecked margins on coloured paper. Dervishes aimed to let go of the ego and focus on love and service, often through dhikr, the repeated remembrance of God. Someone thought this seeker worth a carefully mounted portrait, which says a lot about how much Sufis were respected.

title: Portrait of Emperor Jahangir
summary: Illustrated single work; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1615–20"; matched search q="portrait"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A Mughal emperor is drawn in careful profile, the way coins and medals show rulers. Jahangir ruled India from 1605 to 1627. He was fascinated by nature: he wrote about the birds and animals he saw in his memoir, the Jahangirnama, and had court painters such as Ustad Mansur record them in detail. This portrait from about 1615–20 is ink, opaque watercolour and gold on paper. A ruler who wanted animals painted exactly as they were also had his own face studied closely.

title: Portrait of a Man
summary: Illustrated single work; Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
creator: Riza-yi 'Abbasi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="ca. 1600"; matched search q="portrait"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This is one man, drawn on his own, without a story around him. Around 1600 that was a new idea. Riza-yi ʿAbbasi, court painter to Shah ʿAbbas I in Iran, made single figures like this to be pasted into albums called muraqqa. Before that, Persian painting mostly lived inside illustrated books. The album took over and changed what painters chose to show. Riza used ink, opaque watercolour and gold, and is often called the last great master of the Persian miniature.

title: Duchess of Devonshire Portrait Diamond
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="19th century"; matched search q="portrait"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: You look at this portrait through a diamond. The brooch combines a diamond with a small painting on ivory, and its title, “Duchess of Devonshire Portrait Diamond”, tells you who the sitter is meant to be. A portrait diamond is cut thin and flat, so it works like a sparkling window over a tiny picture. It was made in England in the 1800s. Jewellery like this let people carry a face with them, long before phones or printed photos made that easy.

title: Portrait of Emperor Jahangir Praying
summary: Illustrated single work; Ink and opaque watercolor on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="early 17th century"; matched search q="portrait"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: The most powerful man in India is shown here praying. Jahangir, the Mughal emperor, chose to be painted in a quiet act of devotion rather than on a throne or in battle. He was a careful observer who wrote his own memoir, the Jahangirnama, about his reign and the plants and animals he saw. The painting is early 1600s, in ink and opaque watercolour on paper. Images like this show how rulers wanted to be remembered, and how carefully their painters studied a face.

title: A Portrait of a Statesman
summary: Painting; Opaque watercolor and ink on paper
creator: Yahya Ghaffari
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="dated 1294 AH/1877 CE"; matched search q="portrait"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This is the face of power in 19th-century Iran, painted in 1877 by Yahya Ghaffari, a court painter from a whole family of painters. The Met thinks the sitter may be Amir Kabir, the first prime minister of Nasir al-Din Shah, but that is only a possibility. Ghaffari worked for two Qajar shahs, Naser al-Din and Mozaffar ad-Din, so he was painting the people who ran the country. A portrait like this kept a record of the faces behind the decisions that shaped Iran.

title: Portrait of Emperor Akbar Praying

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This is Akbar, the third Mughal emperor, who ruled from 1556 to 1605 and is often called one of the greatest. Here he prays, with prayer beads. The portrait was painted in the early 1600s, around the time of his death or just after. An emperor shown not on a throne, but praying.

title: Portrait of a Woman

story: A portrait of a woman painted in 16th-century Iran, in tempera on paper. She gets a whole page to herself, which tells you someone thought her worth painting. The record does not say who she is.

story: This letter was written in Egypt in the early 600s, but in Pahlavi, the script of Middle Persian. Why Persian in Egypt? Between 618 and 621 the Sasanian Empire of Iran conquered Egypt and ruled it for a few years. This papyrus is a note from that Persian occupation.

story: A letter fragment on papyrus from Egypt, 600s to 800s. Papyrus kept being used for everyday writing for a long time. The record says little more.

title: Letter in Ta'liq Script

story: This is a real letter, written in 1505 or 1506 in Iran by Darvish 'Abdullah Munshi. It uses ta'liq, the "hanging" script used for official Persian documents. In the 1500s ta'liq began losing ground to nastaliq. So a letter became a work of art, decorated in gold.

title: Fragment of a Letter in Pahlavi Script

story: This piece of a letter, dated 618 to 629, is written in Pahlavi, the script of Middle Persian, yet it was found in Egypt. That date matters. In 618 the Sasanian Empire of Iran invaded Egypt and took it within a few years. So this is a Persian letter from the years when Persia ruled the Nile.

title: "Zal delivers Sam's letter to Manuchihr", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi

story: Zal, one of the greatest warriors of the Shahnama and father of the hero Rostam, delivers a letter from his father Sam to King Manuchihr. The letter matters: Zal wants to marry Rudaba, princess of Kabul. This page was painted in Iran around 1330 to 1340, with gold and silver.

title: "Kai Kavus Upbraids Siyavush in a Letter", Folio 174r from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp

story: King Kai Kavus scolds his own son, Prince Siyavush, by letter. This page is folio 174 of the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, painted in Tabriz around 1525 to 1530. That manuscript had 759 pages and 258 paintings, and was given to the Ottoman sultan in 1568. It was split up in the 1970s, which is why one page can hang in New York.

title: "Mi'raj, The Night Journey of the Prophet," Folio from a Hamla-yi Haidari (Attack of the Lion)

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This page shows the Mi'raj, the Night Journey in which Islamic tradition says the Prophet Muhammad rose to the heavens. It is from a 19th-century Iranian copy of the Hamla-yi Haidari, the Attack of the Lion. The Qur'an only touches the journey in a few verses. The fuller details grew up in later accounts, and painters like this one kept giving them shape.

title: Astrological Drawing Depicting the Constellation Andromeda

story: A 16th-century drawing from Iran of Andromeda, a constellation. Ptolemy listed it in the 100s, and it is named for a princess in Greek myth who was chained to a rock. Al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars, written in Arabic around 964, joined Ptolemy's star list with Arab star lore. Drawings like this kept Greek, Arab and Persian skies together.

title: "Ceasar Captive Before Shapur II", Folio 543r from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp

story: A Roman Caesar, captured, stands before Shapur II, the Sasanian king who ruled so long he held the title from birth until he died at 70. This page is folio 543 of the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, painted around 1530 to 1535 in the royal workshop at Tabriz. The book went to the Ottoman sultan in 1568 and was taken apart in the 1970s.

title: "The Mi'raj or The Night Flight of Muhammad on his Steed Buraq", Folio 3v from a Bustan of Sa`di

story: The Prophet Muhammad's Night Journey, the Mi'raj, riding Buraq. Buraq is a heavenly horse-like creature in Islamic tradition. It is never said to have wings, yet painters almost always gave it some. This page, from around 1525 to 1535, is folio 3 of a copy of Sa'di's Bustan, a book of poems finished in 1257.

story: A silver coin from India dated 1618, with the twins of Gemini. The date falls in the reign of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, who ruled from 1605 to 1627. Jahangir believed in astrology and issued a zodiac series of gold and silver coins, where the sign of the zodiac replaced the name of the month the coin was struck.

story: A pilgrim flask from Kashan, Iran, from the early 1300s, moulded and glazed in blue with zodiac signs in round frames. The zodiac is the band of sky the Sun seems to move along over a year, cut into 12 signs. One catch: parts were added in the early 1900s, so not everything you see is medieval.

title: Group of Zodiac Coins--Aries, Leo, Pisces, Taurus, Capricorn

story: Five silver coins, five star signs: Aries, Leo, Pisces, Taurus and Capricorn, all dated 1617 to 1618 in India. Jahangir, the Mughal emperor from 1605 to 1627, believed in astrology and issued zodiac coins in gold and silver, where the sign of the zodiac replaced the name of the month the coin was struck. So a coin told you the month by its picture.

In a book like this, the writing itself is the art, so calligraphy and gold decoration do the work that pictures do elsewhere. The museum gives few other details.

The record gives few other details, so the craft of the binding and page decoration is what speaks here.

title: Coptic Manuscript
summary: Non-illustrated manuscript; Red, black, and green ink on paper
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="3rd–12th century"; matched search q="manuscript"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This little book is written in Coptic, the last stage of the language of ancient Egypt, spoken by Egyptians from the 3rd century AD. Coptic used the Greek alphabet plus seven extra letters taken from older Egyptian writing. After the Arab conquest, Arabic slowly replaced it as the everyday language. Today nobody grows up speaking Coptic, but priests still use it in church services. So this manuscript, written in red, black and green ink on paper, holds the final chapter of a language that had been spoken for thousands of years.

title: Ewer with Molded Inscription
summary: Ewer; Glass, greenish; mold blown, applied handle
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="9th century"; matched search q="inscription"

story: This little glass jug tells you who made it and who it was for. Its moulded Arabic writing says it was made for the amir in Baghdad, the work of Tayyib ibn Ahmad Barmasi. That means we can meet a 9th-century craftsman by name. It was blown into a mould, a trick glassmakers in the Islamic world inherited from Roman times, so the lettering came out raised on the surface. Baghdad was then the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, and small luxuries like this were made for its elite.

title: Bowl with Inscription
summary: Bowl; Earthenware; painted in black with splashes of green on opaque white (tin) glaze
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="9th century"; matched search q="inscription"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This bowl is a 1,100-year-old answer to a puzzle: how do you make plain clay look like something precious? Potters in 9th-century Nishapur coated earthenware with opaque white tin glaze, then painted writing in black with splashes of green. Some historians think the craze for white-glazed pots in this period was sparked by fine Chinese wares arriving along the trade routes. Nishapur's glazed ceramics became an important trade item, and the Met dug up thousands of objects there between 1935 and 1948. Writing as decoration became one of the great ideas of Islamic art.

title: Textile Fragment with Inscription

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: A cotton fragment from Iraq, 900s or 1000s, painted with ink and gold and bearing an inscription. Painting gold onto cloth was a luxury. The record does not say what the words say.

title: Textile Fragment with Inscription
summary: Textile fragment; Linen, silk; plain weave, tapestry weave
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This piece of linen carries a ruler's name, woven right into the cloth. Made in Egypt around 934 to 940, its band of angular Arabic writing names the caliph al-Radi. Cloths like this are called tiraz. Caliphs had their names put on robes, turbans, cushions and curtains made in official workshops, and gave robes of honour to loyal officials and important guests. Wearing one was like wearing a badge from the top. The idea spread far: Arabic writing in this tradition even ended up on the royal mantle of a Christian king, Roger II of Sicily.

title: Textile Fragment with Inscription
summary: Textile fragment; Linen, silk; plain weave, tapestry weave
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This bit of linen and silk from Egypt, about 934 to 940, carries Arabic writing woven into it. It belongs to the world of tiraz, inscribed textiles. Rulers gave such textiles, often bearing their names, to loyal officials as robes of honour. Wearing one meant you had the ruler's favour.

title: Bowl with Inscription

story: A bowl from 10th-century Iran or Uzbekistan, with an inscription. The potter coated it in white slip, a liquid clay, added black slip and scratched through it to make the design, then sealed it with clear glaze. On bowls like this the writing itself is the decoration. The record does not say what this one reads.

title: Robe
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="19th century"; matched search q="robe"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This robe was made in Bukhara in the 1800s, from silk woven with metal-wrapped thread that would have glittered as its wearer moved. Bukhara was one of the old Silk Road oasis cities, and in the 19th century Bukhara and Samarkand were famous for fine silk ikat, cloth whose threads are tied and dyed in patterns before they are ever woven. A coat like this was a way of wearing your city's wealth and skill on your back. It travelled a long way to New York, where the Met bought it in 1954.

story: A dress could tell you where a woman was from before she said a word. This embroidered silk robe comes from 19th-century Palestine, when knowledgeable people could read a woman's village, and whether she was married or wealthy, from the fabric, colours, cut and stitched patterns of her clothes. Each village had its own motifs, passed down through generations. That embroidery, called tatreez, is still stitched today, in Palestine and around the world, and in 2021 UNESCO added the art of Palestinian embroidery to its list of the world's living heritage.

story: This robe is over 400 years old, and its silk is woven with thread wrapped in metal, so it would have flashed in the light. It was made in Ottoman Turkey in the late 1500s. In the Ottoman world a robe like this, a kaftan, was more than clothing. Its colours, patterns and buttons showed the rank of the person wearing it, and splendid kaftans were handed to ambassadors and honoured guests at Topkapi Palace in Istanbul. A gift of cloth could say you are welcome, you are important, and you belong to us now.

It dates from somewhere between the mid-1800s and the early 1900s and may come from the Balkans. Clothes for small children wear out or get passed down, so a fine one surviving at all is worth noticing. The record says little more.

title: Bowl with Courtly and Astrological Motifs
summary: Bowl; Stonepaste; polychrome inglaze and overglaze painted and gilded on opaque monochrome glaze (mina'i)
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 12th–early 13th century"; matched search q="astronomy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This bowl is painted like a comic strip in glaze: courtly scenes, horses, birds and planets. It is mina'i ware, a kind of pottery from Kashan in Iran. It has been called probably the most luxurious ceramic made in the eastern lands in medieval times. Painters used many colours, fired some under the glaze and some on top, then added gold. The style only lasted a few decades. Production stopped after the Mongol invasion that began in 1219.

title: Kitab suwar al-kawakib al-thabita (Book of the Images of the Fixed Stars) of al-Sufi
summary: Illustrated manuscript; Ink and gold on paper; leather binding
creator: `Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="late 15th century"; matched search q="astronomy"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This book tried to bring together two skies. Around 964, the Persian astronomer ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sufi wrote in Arabic, the shared language of scholars, and combined the star catalogue in Ptolemy's Greek Almagest with the Arabs' own traditions about the constellations. His original copy is lost. The book survives only because people kept copying it carefully, generation after generation. This copy was made in Iran in the late 1400s, in ink and gold on paper, more than 500 years after al-Sufi wrote it. Every copy kept his work alive.

title: Buffware Bowl with Geometric Designs

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This bowl was made in Nishapur around 1,200 years ago, and its bold painted shapes still look fresh. It is buff ware, earthenware painted in several colours under a clear glaze. It was found during the Met's excavations at Nishapur, which uncovered whole neighbourhoods of houses, mosques and bathhouses, and thousands of everyday objects. Bowls like this were what people actually ate from. They show that the city's potters, working on a road that linked Iran with Central Asia and China, were creating a style of their own rather than just copying.

title: Wall Panel with Geometric Interlace
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="15th century"; matched search q="geometric"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This panel is a puzzle made of stone. Its interlacing pattern is built from many pieces of coloured marble, cut and fitted together in 15th-century Cairo. It probably came from the lower part of a wall in a building nobody can now identify. Mamluk builders loved this kind of work, and as stone replaced brick, carving and multicoloured marble mosaic became the main way of decorating walls and floors. The Met notes that similar mosaics decorated mosques, prayer niches and tombs.

title: Panel with Geometric Pattern and Benedictory Inscriptions
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access

scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This panel was carved in Granada, home of the Alhambra, in the late 1200s to mid-1300s. The Nasrid dynasty ruled Granada from 1232 to 1492, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain. Their builders covered walls with geometry and blessings in Arabic. Islamic geometric patterns are built from repeated squares and circles, overlapped and interlaced so they could go on forever. Here limestone is carved into a pattern that wishes good things to whoever reads it.

story: This Qur'an was copied by a prince's own hand. Ibrahim Sultan, a grandson of the conqueror Timur, governed the region of Fars in southern Iran from 1415 to 1435. He was an accomplished artist, a keen calligrapher and a great collector of books. The manuscript is dated 1427 and was probably made in Shiraz, in ink, colour and gold on paper with a leather binding. Copying the Qur'an beautifully was one of the most respected forms of art and devotion, even for a royal.

story: The opening of a book of wisdom poems is laid out in gold. The Bustan, or “Orchard”, was written by the Persian poet Saʿdi in 1257. Its ten chapters, on justice, kindness, love, humility, learning and more, are told through short stories. In India, boys at school had to learn it by heart. This copy was made in Herat in 1514, and the Met names the calligrapher Sultan Muhammad Nur. Its decorated opening tells readers that what follows is precious.

story: This book holds the poems of a ruler, Sultan Husayn Bayqara, who governed Herat from 1469 to 1506. It was copied in 1500, while he was still alive, by Sultan Ali Mashhadi, a master of the flowing nastaliq script. So a king's own verses were written out by one of the best hands of his day, and bound in lacquer.

title: Sitara, Interior Door Curtain of the Ka'ba

story: This curtain once hung on the door inside the Kaʿba in Mecca, the place Muslims around the world face when they pray. It was made in Cairo in 1897–98, in the name of the Ottoman sultan Abdülhamid II. It is silk, heavily embroidered with silver and silver-gilt thread. Every year the Kaʿba is dressed in a new cloth, the kiswah. For centuries the cloth was made in Egypt and carried to Mecca in a procession, a tradition going back to the 1100s.

title: Seal Stone
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access

story: This pink stone is smaller than your thumbnail, and it was someone's signature. Cut into it is a single word, probably a name, which nobody has been able to read yet. Pressed into wax or clay, it marked a letter or a package as truly theirs. People in the Near East had used personal seals like this long before Islam. Carnelian, a tough red-orange stone, was a common choice for them. It was dug up in Nishapur, a great city of medieval Iran.

title: Stamp Seal
source_name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access
locator: department="Islamic Art"; isPublicDomain=true; objectDate="18th century"; matched search q="seal"
scope_basis: Held in the Met's Department of Islamic Art
story: This silver stamp was a signature and a good-luck charm at the same time. A hole in its stem suggests its owner wore it as a pendant. Engraved in its star are the names of the Prophet Muhammad and the first four caliphs, plus the names of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus and their dog, Qitmir. Their miraculous story is told in Surat al-Kahf, the Cave, which people valued for its protective power, so every time this seal was pressed, it left a little of that protection behind on the page.

Look at the tiny beads: they are stamped to look like granulation, an old goldsmith's trick of soldering on tiny balls of metal. It also has gold gilding, loop-in-loop chains, pendants and red carnelian stones. Imagine all of that moving as someone walks.

It is silver, fire-gilded, which means gold was bonded to it with heat, and it carries flower designs, wire chains, pendants and red carnelian stones cut flat on top. It is one of a matching pair.

Openwork, wire chains, pendants and flat-topped carnelians complete it. It was made in Central Asia or Iran in the late 1800s or early 1900s.

It is gilded silver with openwork, chains, little bells and a carnelian stone, from Central Asia or Iran in the late 1800s or early 1900s. Picture the bells jingling as a small boy ran about.

story: This shining silver case was made to carry a Qur'an on the body, as jewellery. It comes from the Turkmen, tribal peoples of Central Asia, and it is covered in gilded openwork, silver beads and flat-cut red carnelians. The Met calls pieces like this the final expression of the Turkmen way of seeing, made as nomadic life was giving way to the modern world in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Its shape echoes the jewelled boxes of royal courts, but its boldness is all Turkmen. It is faith, wealth and identity worn where everyone could see them.

story: A triangular silver case for an amulet. People kept prayers or protective charms inside cases like this. It hangs on twisted wire chains with bells and has raised patterns and flat-cut carnelian stones. It was made in Central Asia or Iran in the late 1800s or early 1900s.

story: Read this screen as a puzzle: letters and plant shapes are cut right through the clay, so light comes through between them. It was made, probably in Iran, in the 1100s from stonepaste, a body of ground quartz and glass with a little clay, then painted and glazed. Calligraphy is one of the main forms of Islamic art, and here it does a second job as part of a window. The Met also keeps fragments of a second screen like it, so it may not have been the only one.

title: "Laila and Majnun at School", Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami of Ganja

story: Two children meet at school and fall in love: that is how one of the most famous love stories in the Islamic world begins. Layla and Majnun started as an Arab tale about a 7th-century poet. The Persian poet Nizami turned it into a long poem in 1188, and from there it spread into Persian, Turkish and Indian languages. This page was made in Herat in 1431–32. The Met names Jaʿfar Baisunghuri, whose name ties him to Prince Baysunghur, the leading patron of Persian painting at the time. Look for the pupils and their teacher.

story: Layla and Majnun is an old Arab love story about a poet named Qays and a girl named Layla. It became one of the most famous romances in the Islamic world. This page from Herat, dated 1524 to 1525, shows them as children at school. The museum tags it with books, children and reading: a love story that starts in a classroom.

title: Chastisement of a Pupil

story: Some school scenes never change. In this 1605–06 album page from Mashhad, Iran, the artist Muhammad Qasim shows a teacher punishing a pupil. It is a small, human moment, painted in ink, watercolour and gold. Pages like this were made for albums (muraqqa), which by the late 1500s had become the main way people in Iran collected paintings. Painters began to show everyday life, not just heroes and kings. Look closely and you might recognise the expressions.
