story: This panel is cedar wood, carved and painted with scalloped, or “cusped”, arches. It comes from 14th-century Morocco, when the Marinid dynasty ruled much of the Maghreb. The Marinids were of Berber origin but culturally Arabised, and they were strongest in the mid-1300s, around when this panel was made. Wooden panels like this were part of buildings, high above people's heads, and were meant to be seen from below. The source gives little more, so look at how the arches repeat.

story: A sultan moves in procession, with elephants. Ibrahim ʿAdil Shah II ruled Bijapur in the Deccan, in central India, from 1580 to 1627. He was a skilful administrator, a poet, an artist and a generous patron, and he was tolerant of other religions. Deccan painting is known for brilliant colour and an air of luxury. The Met dates this album page to the mid-1600s and credits it to ʿAli Riza ʿAbbasi. It shows how a court wanted to remember its king.

title: A Chinese Serow (Capricornis milneedwardsi argyrochaetes)

story: This is a careful animal portrait, painted around 1800, probably in Calcutta. The animal is a serow, a goat-antelope from the Himalayas and the mountains of Southeast Asia and China. Indian artists working for officials of the East India Company made natural history paintings like this, often life-size. They mixed the fine detail of Mughal and Rajput painting with European ideas about depth and volume, a mix now called “Company style”. Look at the fur: every hair seems counted.

story: This is a copy of the Shahnama, the Book of Kings, made in 1606 or 1607 in what is now Afghanistan. Ferdowsi wrote the poem around 1000 CE. It has some 50,000 couplets, which makes it one of the world's longest epic poems, and it tells Iran's past from the creation of the world. This copy is painted with silver and gold and has a lacquer binding.

story: A full Shahnama made in Iran between 1663 and 1669, painted with colour, silver and gold. That is six years of work for one copy of a poem with some 50,000 couplets. The Shahnama is Iran's national epic.

title: Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi

story: A book made twice. The text of this Shahnama was copied in 1602, but the paintings, decoration and binding were added in the 1800s in India. So two centuries separate its words from its pictures. The poem itself, by Ferdowsi, is one of the longest epics ever written by one author.

title: "Rustam Lassos Rakhsh", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings)

story: Every hero needs the right horse. This page shows Rustam, the greatest hero of the Persian Book of Kings, lassoing the colt Rakhsh. In the poem, Rakhsh has the chest of a lion and the strength of an elephant, and no one but Rustam ever rides him. The painting was made around 1450, and the Met attributes it to India, even though its style looks deeply Persian. That tells you how far Persian stories and painting spread. The tale of a boy choosing his horse travelled from Iran to India and still works on readers today.

story: This album is a 1790 street guide to the people of Istanbul. Its 67 watercolour portraits show Ottoman officials, soldiers, sailors, traders and women, each with a caption in Italian. The Met says the painter was Greek, perhaps someone trained in painting religious icons. Its pictures let us see what people in the Ottoman capital actually wore more than two centuries ago. The Met only bought it in 2024, so this album of everyday faces is one of its newest arrivals, and a reminder that a city is its people as much as its palaces.

story: This dish was a peace message from Poland to the Ottoman sultan. In 1776 King Stanislaw August Poniatowski ordered a huge dinner service from his own pottery in Warsaw as a diplomatic gift for Sultan Abdul Hamid I. Its Ottoman Turkish inscriptions say the present was sent from the King of the Lekhs at Warsaw as a token of respect. The painting copies Chinese and Japanese porcelain, which both kings loved. Of 280 pieces made, 160 reached Topkapi Palace in Istanbul, and about 100 survive, scattered across Istanbul, Warsaw, London and New York.

story: This dish comes from Iznik, a town in Turkey whose potters tried to match the most precious tableware on earth: Chinese porcelain. They could not make porcelain, so they invented their own answer, a white body of silica and glass painted under a clear glaze. Over the 1500s they added turquoise, green and, from around 1560, a brilliant bright red. The same workshops made the tiles for the great mosques of the architect Sinan. Strangely, most surviving Iznik dishes are now in museums outside Turkey.

story: This simple glazed dish was dug up in the ruins of Ctesiphon, one of the great capitals of the ancient world. It was a royal capital of the Sasanian Persian empire. After the Muslim conquest it faded, and by the end of the 8th century, around when this dish was made, its people had mostly moved on. Baghdad, built nearby, took its place. This dish is from the city's last chapter.

story: This tile was made in Spain in the second half of the 1400s. Look closely at the recipe: the potters painted it with cobalt blue on an opaque white glaze, then powdered gold over it, and sealed it all under a clear glaze. That is a lot of work for one square of wall. Spanish pottery in this tradition, called Hispano-Moresque ware, began under Muslim rule in al-Andalus and kept going under Christian kings. For a long time it was the most luxurious pottery made in Europe.

story: This tile is dated 1421 and comes from Bursa, the Ottoman capital before Constantinople was taken in 1453. It uses cuerda seca, Spanish for “dry cord”: waxy lines kept the coloured glazes from running into one another, and the tile was then gilded. Bursa's Green Mosque, built for Sultan Mehmed I, takes its name from the green and blue tiles inside it. This tile shows the colour and craft Bursa was capable of in those years.

The base material is stonepaste, a mix of ground glass and clay that can be fired at a lower heat than clay alone. The museum record does not tell us what building it came from.

story: This whole prayer niche is made from many small pieces of tile. It was made in Isfahan in 1354–55. A mihrab is a niche in a mosque wall that shows the direction of the Kaʿba in Mecca, which Muslims face when they pray. Craftsmen cut glazed tiles into small shapes, fitted them together like a jigsaw, and set them in mortar. The Met notes Arabic inscriptions on it. Every curve had to be planned before a single piece was cut.

story: This tile has a date in it: 722 in the Islamic calendar, or 1322 to 1323. It came from a mihrab, the niche in a mosque wall that shows the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which people face to pray. It is moulded with Arabic writing. So this tile once helped point a whole room of people toward Mecca.

title: "Mihrab Vents His Anger Upon Sindukht", Folio 83v from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp

story: Mihrab, king of Kabul, is furious with his wife Sindukht because their daughter Rudaba has fallen for Zal. This page, folio 83, is from the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, maybe the most fully illustrated copy of the epic ever made. In the end the couple marry, and their son is Rostam, the main hero of the whole Shahnama.

story: King Manuchihr welcomes the warrior Sam, then orders him to go to war against Mihrab of Kabul. Why? Sam's son Zal loves Mihrab's daughter. This is folio 80 of the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, painted around 1525 in Tabriz. The manuscript once had 258 paintings; its pages are now spread across collections worldwide.

story: Zal questions his father Sam about his plans for the house of Mihrab, whose daughter Rudaba Zal loves. It is folio 81 of the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, painted around 1525 to 1530. Turn back two pages in the original book, folio 80 is Manuchihr ordering war on Mihrab. The Met has both. The love story wins: Zal and Rudaba become the parents of Rostam.

story: This is a playlist in book form, made in the 1500s. It gathers favourite poems by several Persian poets, including Amir Shahi of Sabzavar, Jami and Nasir Khusraw, into one volume. Its cover is painted lacquer, so even the outside is a small painting. Gathering favourite poems from different writers in one book let a reader carry a whole library of voices in one hand. Reading it is a bit like flipping through someone's saved songs from five centuries ago.

It has no pictures, but its pages use ink, watercolour and gold, and its leather cover is painted with gold too. Even a book of words was made to be beautiful.

It was made using cuerda seca, Spanish for "dry cord". Potters drew black wax lines between the colours so the different glazes would not run into each other. Put the tiles together and you get a painting on a wall that does not fade.

story: This album holds the handwriting of one of the great masters of Islamic calligraphy. Sheikh Hamdullah was born in Amasya in 1436 and became the leading calligrapher of the Ottoman world. This album from about 1500, probably made in Istanbul, gathers poetry and sayings of the Prophet (hadith) in his hand. The pages sit in borders of marbled paper inside a leather and gold binding. Albums like this were made to be admired, studied and copied, and students learned by imitating pages like these.

story: This book holds the poems of Ibn al-Farid, an Arab poet born in Cairo who was called the greatest mystic poet of the Arabs. Some of his poems are said to have been written in states of ecstasy. This copy was made in Iran in 1595, painted with gold and bound in gold-stamped leather. A Cairo poet, read and recopied in Iran: poetry crossing borders by hand.

story: This book is poetry written in Turkic at a time when most great poets wrote in Persian. Ali-Shir Nava'i, a poet and statesman in Herat, believed his own Chagatai Turkic language was just as good for poetry, and even wrote a book comparing the two languages. This copy of his collected poems was written out in Herat in 1499 to 1500 by Sultan 'Ali al-Mashhadi, the city's most famous calligrapher, who worked for Nava'i himself. Today many people across the Turkic world see Nava'i as a founder of their literature, and a city in Uzbekistan is named after him.

story: Men whirl in a circle while music plays. This page, painted in Herat around 1480, illustrates the poems of Hafiz, the 14th-century poet whose verses many Iranians still learn by heart and quote as everyday sayings. The scene connects to sama, the Sufi practice of “listening”: remembering God through music, poetry and movement. One famous form, the Mevlevi ceremony of Turkey, is recognised by UNESCO. The painter has caught the dance mid-turn.

The poems are by Mahmud ʿAbd al-Baqi, known by his pen name Baki, who lived from 1526 to 1600 and was called the “Sultan of poets”. This painting comes from a copy made in Turkey in the late 1500s. It shows that Ottoman poetry books could hold history and power as well as love poems. Look at how the painter fits a crowd into one small page.

story: This painting shows the royal stables in Isfahan. In the upper half of the work, the Persian king, or shah (sitting next to the column on the right), has gathered on a platform with five kneeling courtiers and various attendants serving fruit and wine. The king is identified in the artist’s signature at the upper left as Shah ‘Abbas II, who died in 1666, before this painting was executed. Persian painters worked on highly polished paper and often framed their pictures with ruled lines of gold or colour.

Its bands are inlaid with silver Arabic writing, so tangled into leaves that nobody has yet read it: the maker chose beauty over legibility. Above one eye hole is a Turkic tribal mark, a tamga.

Iznik potters started out copying Chinese blue-and-white porcelain, but by the 1550s, working with the sultan's own design studio, they had made a style that stood for the whole Ottoman Empire. Tulips were a real craze too, grown in Istanbul's gardens.

story: This mosque in Tehran was founded by a princess and designed by a Russian.
